pages.name: The spring
pages.text: A 1 kg mass hangs on a spring, beside a damper. Its weight is balanced at rest, so only the extra pull counts. It is lifted 0.5 m and let go. Ideally, that pull grows in step with its height `x`. The drag grows in step with its speed. Newton's second law gives `m x″ = −k x − c x′`, with [[stiffness]] `k` and [[damping]] `c`. All on one side: `m x″ + c x′ + k x = 0`. It is [[second-order]], because `x″` is its highest derivative.

pages.name: Let go
pages.task: At the moment it is let go, the mass is still. What is its acceleration?
pages.why: It is still, so the damper's drag is 0. The net pull of spring and weight is 4 × 0.5 = 2 N, back towards rest. So `m x″` = −2 N. With 1 kg, that makes `x″` = −2 m/s², downward. It speeds up even though its speed is zero.

pages.name: The circuit
pages.text: Now a loop holds a 1 H coil, a 0.5 Ω resistor and a 0.25 F capacitor. The capacitor starts with 0.5 C on it, which is 2 V. The switch closes and current flows. With no supply, the volts round the loop add to zero. The coil drops `L q″`, the resistor `R q′` and the capacitor `q ÷ C`. Here `q′` is the current. So `L q″ + R q′ + q ÷ C = 0`, and the charge traces the same kind of curve.

pages.task: Which capacitor matches a stiffer spring?
pages.why: In the two rules, `k` sits where `1 ÷ C` sits. A stiffer spring has a bigger `k`, so it needs a bigger `1 ÷ C`. That means a smaller `C`. A smaller capacitor gives more volts for the same charge, so it pushes back harder.

pages.name: Which way?
pages.task: While its trace runs across, which way does the mass move?
pages.why: The mass only moves up and down on its spring. The trace runs across because time does. Each point records the mass's height at one moment. So the curve is a record of height against time, not a path.

pages.text: Each term has a job. [[Inertia]] resists a change in motion. [[Loss]] turns energy into heat. [[Store]] holds energy and pushes back. The three always add to zero. That sum is the equation itself, read at one instant.

pages.task: At 1 s the loss bar reads −0.36 N and the store bar −0.45 N. What does the inertia bar read?
pages.why: The three terms add to zero at every moment. Store plus loss is −0.45 − 0.36 = −0.81 N. So inertia must be 0.81 N. It is positive because the mass is below rest and still falling. The spring pulls it up and the damper drags it up.

pages.name: Two starts
pages.text: The mass is let go twice from 0.5 m. Once it starts at rest. Once it starts with a push of 1 m/s downward. The mass drawn is the pushed run. The two traces part at once. The rule gives the acceleration from the height and the speed. So a [[second-order]] equation needs two starting values, the height and the speed. In the circuit, those are the capacitor's charge and the coil's current.

pages.name: An empty capacitor
pages.task: Now the capacitor starts empty, with 0.8 A flowing in the coil. What happens next?
pages.answer: The coil keeps the current flowing, so charge builds
pages.why: A coil fights any change in its current, as a mass fights a change in its speed. So the 0.8 A keeps flowing at first, and charge builds on the capacitor. That charge pushes back and slows the current. Then the loop swings, like a mass pushed from its rest point.

pages.task: Near 4.75 s the mass is still for an instant, at the bottom of a swing. The store bar reads −0.61 N. What do the other two read?
pages.why: Still means no speed, so the loss term is 0 N. The three terms still add to zero. So inertia is 0.61 N, upward. The spring pulls the mass back up towards rest.
